questions.text: Consider a system with 2 KB direct mapped data cache with a block size of 64 bytes. The system has a physical address space of 64 KB and a word length of 16 bits. During the execution of a program, four data words P, Q, R, and S are accessed in that order 10 times (i.e., PQRSPQRS...). Hence, there are 40 accesses to data cache altogether. Assume that the data cache is initially empty and no other data words are accessed by the program. The addresses of the first bytes of P, Q, R, and S are 0xA248, 0xC28A, 0xCA8A, and 0xA262, respectively. For the execution of the above program, which of the following statements is/are TRUE with respect to the data cache?
questions.solution:
Lines = 2 KB / 64 B = 32. Address 16 bits = tag 5 | index 5 | offset 6. Block number = address / 64; line = block mod 32.
- P = 0xA248 [latex]\rightarrow[/latex] block 649 [latex]\rightarrow[/latex] line 9
- Q = 0xC28A [latex]\rightarrow[/latex] block 778 [latex]\rightarrow[/latex] line 10
- R = 0xCA8A [latex]\rightarrow[/latex] block 810 [latex]\rightarrow[/latex] line 10
- S = 0xA262 [latex]\rightarrow[/latex] block 649 [latex]\rightarrow[/latex] line 9 (same block as P)

- S is always accessed after P has loaded that block [latex]\rightarrow[/latex] every S access is a hit True
- Line 9 is used only by P/S [latex]\rightarrow[/latex] P is never evicted True
- Q and R share line 10 [latex]\rightarrow[/latex] every R access evicts Q True
- At the end, P's block (with S) and R are in the cache, not "only R and S" False

Answer: Options 1, 2 and 4

Click here for detail solution by gateoverflow
options: Every access to S is a hit.
Once P is brought to the cache it is never evicted.
At the end of the execution only R and S reside in the cache.
Every access to R evicts Q from the cache.

questions.text: Consider a digital display system (DDS) shown in the figure that displays the contents of register X. A 16-bit code word is used to load a word in X, either from S or from R. S is a 1024-word memory segment and R is a 32-word register file. Based on the value of mode bit M, T selects an input word to load in X. P and Q interface with the corresponding bits in the code word to choose the addressed word. Which one of the following represents the functionality of P, Q, and T?
questions.solution:
Match each block with its job:
- S has 1024 words, so the S-address is 10 bits. P must activate exactly one of 1024 words [latex]\rightarrow[/latex] 10 : [latex]2^{10}[/latex] decoder.
- R has 32 words, so the R-address is 5 bits [latex]\rightarrow[/latex] Q is a 5 : [latex]2^5[/latex] decoder.
- T chooses one of two inputs (from S or R) using mode bit M [latex]\rightarrow[/latex] 2 : 1 multiplexer.

Answer: P is 10:2^10 decoder; Q is 5:2^5 decoder; T is 2:1 multiplexer

Click here for detail solution by gateoverflow

questions.text: A cache memory that has a hit rate of 0.8 has an access latency 10 ns and miss penalty 100 ns. An optimization is done on the cache to reduce the miss rate. However, the optimization results in an increase of cache access latency to 15 ns, whereas the miss penalty is not affected. The minimum hit rate (rounded off to two decimal places) needed after the optimization such that it should not increase the average memory access time is _____.
questions.solution:
Average memory access time = hit latency + miss rate [latex]\times[/latex] miss penalty.

Before: [latex]10+0.2\times100=30[/latex] ns.
After: [latex]15+(1-h)\times100\le30\Rightarrow1-h\le0.15\Rightarrow h\ge0.85[/latex]

Answer: 0.85

Click here for detail solution by gateoverflow

questions.text: Let WB and WT be two set associative cache organizations that use LRU algorithm for cache block replacement. WB is a write back cache and WT is a write through cache. Which of the following statements is/are FALSE?
questions.solution:
Check each statement (we need the FALSE ones):
- "Each block in WB and WT has a dirty bit": WT writes memory on every write, so it needs no dirty bit [latex]\text{---}[/latex] FALSE.
- "Every write hit in WB transfers data to memory": WB only sets the dirty bit; memory is updated on eviction [latex]\text{---}[/latex] FALSE.
- "Eviction from WT causes no transfer to memory": memory is already up to date [latex]\text{---}[/latex] TRUE.
- "A read miss in WB never evicts a dirty block": the LRU victim can be dirty [latex]\text{---}[/latex] FALSE.

Answer: Options 1, 2 and 4

Click here for detail solution by gateoverflow
options: Each cache block in WB and WT has a dirty bit.
Every write hit in WB leads to a data transfer from cache to main memory.
Eviction of a block from WT will not lead to data transfer from cache to main memory.
A read miss in WB will never lead to eviction of a dirty block from WB.

questions.text: Which one of the following facilitates transfer of bulk data from hard disk to main memory with the highest throughput?
questions.solution:
In DMA, the DMA controller moves the whole block between disk and memory directly, without the CPU handling every word. Interrupt-driven, polling and programmed I/O all need the CPU for each word, so they are much slower for bulk data.

Answer: DMA based I/O transfer
